Neonatal Dusky sharks emerge from their mothers at a total length of 78 cm [Lb = 78 cm], a size that reflects an extended period of intrauterine development. This substantial length at birth provides newborn pups with a degree of protection against predators that smaller elasmobranchs lack. Field surveys in the western North Atlantic consistently record neonates in shallow coastal nurseries, where they remain for the first few years of life. The age of these newborn individuals at the moment of parturition has been estimated under controlled thermal conditions, with data indicating a gestation period of approximately 701.5 days [ab = approximately 701.5 days] when maintained at a mean water temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. This remarkably long gestation, spanning about 23 months, is among the most protracted recorded for any carcharhinid species and is thought to be linked to the large size of the pups at birth. The thermal environment clearly plays a regulatory role; at lower temperatures, metabolic rates are suppressed, slowing foetal growth and prolonging the developmental timeline. Consequently, females in cooler, temperate waters may exhibit slightly longer gestation periods than those inhabiting subtropical regions, though the reported figure of roughly 23 months at 15 °C [T = 15 °C] serves as a representative baseline for the species.

Juvenile Dusky sharks grow relatively slowly compared to many other large-bodied requiem sharks, a pattern that is reflected in the substantial time required to achieve reproductive maturity. The interval from birth to the onset of sexual maturity has been quantified in long-term tagging studies, which indicate that approximately 7300 days since birth [tp = approximately 7300 days since birth] elapse before a young individual begins to produce at a temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C]viable gametes. Such a protracted pre-reproductive phase, recorded in populations inhabiting waters at 13 °C [T = 13 °C], carries profound demographic consequences: a female must survive two decades of natural and fishing-related mortality before she can contribute to the next generation. The total length corresponding to this pubertal milestone is approximately 235 cm [Lp = approximately 235 cm], though regional variation is considerable, with published values ranging from 220 cm to 300 cm depending on local environmental conditions and population density. Males typically mature at a slightly smaller size than females, a common pattern in sexually dimorphic sharks.

Once females attain sexual maturity, their reproductive output is constrained by both the frequency of parturition and the number of pups produced per litter. The maximum annual reproductive rate for this species, derived from observations of females in the western South Atlantic, is approximately 10 pups per year [Ri = approximately 10 pups per year] when calculated across consecutive breeding seasons under an average thermal regime of 13 °C [T = 13 °C]. However, litter size is notoriously variable; published accounts document clutches ranging from as few as 3 pups to as many as 14 pups per pregnancy [N_R_i = 3 pups to as many as 14 pups per pregnancy], with the frequency of pupping events generally estimated at one litter every two to three years [F_R_i = one litter every two to three years]. This low reproductive frequency, combined with the moderate litter size, yields a very low intrinsic rate of population increase compared to teleost fishes or even many other shark species. The cool thermal conditions associated with these estimates, 13 °C [T = 13 °C], are typical of the continental shelf waters this species frequents during its reproductive migrations. Such a conservative life-history strategy renders the Dusky shark exceptionally vulnerable to overfishing, as populations cannot withstand even moderate levels of adult mortality.

The maximum attainable body size in the Dusky shark, reported from verified captures and museum specimens, reaches an ultimate total length of 420 cm [Li = 420 cm]. Corresponding to this impressive length, the ultimate wet weight of the largest recorded individuals is 347000 grams [Wwi = 347000 grams], representing a massive body mass that places Carcharhinus obscurus among the heaviest members of its genus. These top-end measurements are almost exclusively associated with large, mature females, which consistently outgrow males in both length and mass. Attaining such a size requires sustained somatic growth over many decades, a trajectory that is directly linked to the species' slow maturation and long lifespan. The energetic demands of supporting a body mass of 347 kilograms [Wwi = 347 kilograms] are substantial, particularly for a warm-bodied, active predator that undertakes extensive seasonal migrations along continental margins. Comparative data from related species, such as the silky shark and the bull shark, suggest that the Dusky shark's ultimate length is near the upper boundary for the genus, a distinction that likely confers competitive advantages in prey acquisition but also increases susceptibility to entanglement in fishing gear designed for large pelagic fishes.

Longevity records for the Dusky shark indicate that individuals can survive for up to 14600 days [am = up to 14600 days] in the wild, a figure equivalent to approximately 40 years, based on tag-recapture studies conducted in coastal waters maintaining an average temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C]. This extended lifespan, lasting around 4 decades [am = 4 decades], is consistent with the species' slow growth, late maturity, and low fecundity, forming a cohesive slow life-history syndrome. Interestingly, the 40-year maximum longevity (40 years) [am = 40 years] at 13 °C [T = 13 °C] appears to be a thermal optimum; populations inhabiting warmer, more productive waters may experience slightly reduced lifespans due to accelerated metabolic ageing, whereas those in colder regions may live longer but grow even more slowly. The interplay between temperature and lifespan is a critical consideration for fisheries management, as models parameterised with a lifespan of 40 years [am = 40 years] predict substantially slower population recovery rates than those for shorter-lived species at a temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C].
